newsitem.title: FRANCE: Franc seen staying firm after overnight dip.
newsitem.headline: Franc seen staying firm after overnight dip.

text.p: The franc will probably stay firm after rebounding from its latest dip early Wednesday in reaction to stronger-than-expected German economic data, economists said on Thursday.

They said the franc's tumble, which took it to 3.4315 per mark before the Bank of France was reported to have intervened to support it, was an overreaction because the French and German economic situations were not as different as headline gross domestic product figures suggested.
"There's some sticker shock," Smith Barney economist Steven Englander said. "When you juxtapose the German and French GDP numbers, people get nervous."
At 1423 GMT, the franc was trading at 3.4236 per mark, back at the levels it was trading it before the German data.
But, Englander said, "the German economy isn't that strong and the French economy isn't that weak."
"At the end of the day, the progress of these economies is not that different," agreed Nomura economist Sonja Gibbs. "In fact France has some positives that Germany doesn't."
On Wednesday, France reported that its economy shrank 0.4 percent in the second quarter. On Thursday Germany reported its economy grew 1.5 percent, beyond most economists' expectations.
Economists said a comparison of the two economies over the first six months of the year showed they were growing at a much more similar pace.
"The fundamental outlook for the two economies is not that different. It's really a question of timing," Gibbs said.
French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on Thursday that the two economies were growing at the same pace.

"Our economies are on the same growth trend, a trend which should inspire confidence," he said after a lunch with Prime Minister Alain Juppe. "What is clear is in the first half, we had growth of 0.7 percent and the Gemans are on the same level," he said.

While acknowledging that markets doubt France's economic health and its ability to cut its deficit-to-GDP ratio to three percent in time for monetary union, economists believe speculation against the franc will prove futile longer term.

Englander said the use of one-time measures such as a 37.5 billion franc payment from France Telecom and payments from state-owned bank Caisse des Depots et Consignation showed that France is deadly serious about meeting targets to take part in the launch of the single currency and should smooth the franc's performance in the months ahead.

"The franc may have some rough going for the next few weeks but the fact that you're seeing all this one-time stuff thrown into the budget means they're going for it," he said. "My guess is that when they set the (currency) parities for EMU, the franc is going to be stronger than 3.43 per mark," Englander said.
Economists in France also point out there is less likelihood this autumn of labour unrest as severe as the transport strike which nearly crippled the country last year.
Some of the country's biggest labour unions, while warning that many of the ingredients for trouble are present, have been hesitant to predict a major explosion of strikes and unrest.

"If there are no surprises in the budget or in the social security situation, the franc should stay between 3.41 per mark and 3.43 per mark," Credit Lyonnais economist Valerie Asselot said. "I am not worried, I do not expext a franc crisis."
